name: Gwlad y Tylwyth Teg
text: Gwlad y Tylwyth Teg is the Welsh phrase for the land of the fair folk. In everyday speech the same words can also name sleep or the grave. The phrase points to the home of the Tylwyth Teg, the fairies of Welsh custom. It thus links a place of the imagination with the country of the dead. MacKillop enters gwlad as a Welsh word for land or country. The term may name an independent small kingdom in Wales before 1282, the year of the English conquest. The term may also name a cultural region. There folk with a common dialect and a common set of customs dwelt for ages. The reader may consult T. M. Charles-Edwards for the broader scholarly treatment of gwlad. His 1993 Oxford study, called Early Irish and Welsh Kinship, sets the kinship field alongside the land-word. MacKillop notes that the same article gwarwyn a throt once served as a hidden name. It served in Monmouthshire, now Gwent. It named the tylwyth teg, the Welsh fairy folk. That nickname, meaning the white-naped one with the trot, kept the fairy folk out of plain speech.
